summary: This informational RFC provides a threat analysis of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), examining how it might be attacked.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP uses mappings to connect endpoint identifiers with routing locators. This RFC describes how attackers could misuse those mappings and messages, and how operators can reduce the risks.

questions: what are the security threats to lisp
how can lisp map-reply be abused
subtitle: Threats to the Locator/ID Separation Protocol when used in an untrusted network.

tldr.problem: The LISP specifications need to be considered in a public network where attackers may be on or off the communication path and may target control or data functions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines attacker modes and threat categories, examines attack vectors in LISP messages and forwarding features, and discusses mitigations.
tldr.outcome: It advises filtering, rate limiting, authentication where possible, and verifying information learned from packets before relying on it.

today: RFC 7835 is an Informational document published in April 2016. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope of the Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) separates endpoint identifiers from routing locators. This RFC analyzes security threats if the current LISP specifications are deployed in the public Internet.

It focuses on unicast LISP, including interworking, the Map-Server, and Map-Versioning. It does not cover every possible LISP use or threats caused by particular implementations, and it assumes readers know the base LISP documents.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP separates the identifier for an endpoint from the locator used to route packets to it. This RFC examines threats to the specified LISP mechanisms in a public network.

sections.title: Attacker Modes and Threat Categories
sections.content:
The RFC considers attackers inside or outside a LISP site, on or off the packet path, and operating in the control or data plane. An attacker may also stop transmitting while an effect it caused continues. These modes can be combined.

Threat categories include replay, packet manipulation, interception, spoofing, rogue information, denial of service, performance attacks, intrusion, amplification, passive monitoring, and combinations of these. With encapsulation, an attacker may forge an inner endpoint identifier, an outer routing locator, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may be inside or outside a site and may observe packets or inject their own. The RFC groups attacks by what they do, including replaying, changing, or spoofing packets.

sections.title: Attacks on Forwarding and Mapping
sections.content:
Gleaning lets a tunnel router learn an identifier-to-locator mapping from packets. A forged packet could cause an unverified mapping to redirect traffic. Locator Status Bits and Map-Version information can also influence locator selection or trigger control messages.

Map-Request messages can consume mapping-system resources when sent at a high rate. Map-Reply messages can install mappings in a router's cache; the nonce helps connect a reply to a request but does not validate the reply's contents. A valid Egress Tunnel Router can also claim a prefix beyond the one assigned to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some LISP features let routers learn mappings or request updated ones. Attackers may misuse these features to redirect traffic, fill caches, or generate excess control messages.

sections.title: Mitigation and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC recommends careful deployment, filtering, enabling only needed features, and checking information obtained from other parties. Authentication should be used for mapping messages and exchanges within the mapping system where possible. Actions in the control plane triggered by data-plane packets should be rate limited.

Information learned from packet fields or gleaning should not be trusted immediately. For example, a reachability change can trigger a rate-limited test, and a newly gleaned mapping can be limited to the flow that caused it until it is verified. Public LISP mappings can also reveal information about network infrastructure and reachable sites.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should limit message rates and verify mappings before using them broadly. Public mappings may also reveal information about the network's edge routers.
